name: HELIX syndrome (CLDN10)
aliases: hypohidrosis electrolyte imbalance lacrimal gland dysfunction ichthyosis xerostomia

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive multisystem disorder caused by variants in CLDN10, encoding the tight-junction protein claudin-10 in the thick ascending limb and exocrine glands
The acronym captures the phenotype: Hypohidrosis, Electrolyte imbalance, Lacrimal gland dysfunction, Ichthyosis, and Xerostomia
Renal involvement produces a salt-losing tubulopathy with hypokalaemic alkalosis and hypermagnesaemia rather than the hypomagnesaemia seen in most other tubulopathies
Reduced sweating and impaired tear and saliva production reflect claudin-10 loss in exocrine gland epithelia
Affected individuals may present with heat intolerance, dry eyes and mouth, and scaly skin from early life
Management is supportive with electrolyte correction, attention to overheating and dehydration, ocular lubrication, and skin care
Consider HELIX in a child with a salt-wasting tubulopathy accompanied by dry eyes, dry mouth, and reduced sweating, and confirm with CLDN10 testing
reference.pathophysiology: Claudin-10 is a tight-junction protein that governs paracellular ion permeability. The kidney-relevant isoform (claudin-10b) forms a paracellular sodium pathway in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, and its loss shifts paracellular selectivity towards divalent cations. This impairs paracellular sodium reabsorption, causing renal salt wasting with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, while enhanced paracellular magnesium and calcium transport leads to the characteristic hypermagnesaemia and reduced calcium excretion. In exocrine glands, defective claudin-10 disrupts fluid secretion, explaining hypohidrosis, reduced lacrimation, and xerostomia, and abnormal epidermal barrier function underlies the ichthyosis.
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes showing hypokalaemia and unusually raised magnesium
Venous blood gas confirming metabolic alkalosis
Urinary electrolyte studies documenting renal salt wasting
Assessment of tear production (Schirmer test) and salivary flow
Sweat testing and dermatological evaluation of the skin barrier
redFlags: Hyperthermia and dehydration during heat exposure or febrile illness
Severe symptomatic hypokalaemia with arrhythmia risk
Corneal damage from chronic dry eyes
Failure to thrive from combined salt loss and reduced intake
reference.prognosis: The tubulopathy and exocrine features are generally manageable with supportive care and long-term renal function is usually preserved, but chronic sicca symptoms, heat intolerance, and skin involvement require ongoing multidisciplinary attention.
pitfalls: Expecting hypomagnesaemia and being misled by the hypermagnesaemia that distinguishes HELIX
Overlooking the extrarenal exocrine features when a tubulopathy dominates the presentation
Failing to counsel about heat intolerance and dehydration risk
Mistaking the sicca picture for an acquired autoimmune process
management: Correct the salt-losing tubulopathy with potassium replacement and sodium and fluid repletion to counter hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, avoiding magnesium supplementation given the characteristic hypermagnesaemia
Protect against heat intolerance and dehydration from hypohidrosis with cooling measures, adequate hydration and avoidance of overheating
Manage sicca features with regular ocular lubricants and artificial tears for lacrimal failure and saliva substitutes with meticulous dental care for xerostomia
Treat the ichthyosis with emollients and keratolytic skin care
Monitor serum electrolytes, magnesium and long-term renal function periodically
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across nephrology, ophthalmology, dermatology and clinical genetics
Offer genetic counselling and family screening given autosomal recessive CLDN10 inheritance
